BEYOND THE REHEARSAL : Series 3 Beyond the Platform: Building a Choir That Serves God With Purpose We have come to the final part of this series, Beyond the Rehearsal: When the Song Becomes a Lifeline. In Series One, we explored how a choir rehearsal can have an impact beyond the church walls. In Series Two, we considered the importance of preparing the singer, not just the song. Now, we must confront a deeper question: Are we building choirs that can sing for God, or choirs that are intentional about serving God through their singing? There is a difference. A choir can have excellent voices, accurate harmonies, coordinated movements, and impressive musical arrangements. Yet, the most important question remains: Is the choir conscious of the spiritual responsibility behind its assignment? Gospel music is not simply music performed in a church. It communicates spiritual truths, proclaims the message of the gospel, encourages faith, and creates opportunities for people to reflect on their relationship with God. Therefore, our preparation must go beyond musical ability. It must include spiritual understanding, personal devotion, godly character, and a sincere desire to serve. Spiritual Preparation Must Come Before Public Presentation It is possible to prepare a song thoroughly without preparing ourselves spiritually. We can learn every note, memorise every word, master every harmony, and still approach the ministration as nothing more than a performance. Musical preparation is important. God deserves the best of our abilities. But spiritual preparation reminds us why we are using those abilities in the first place. A choir should not wait until it stands before a congregation before remembering that it is serving God. Spiritual preparation begins in private. It includes prayer, studying God’s Word, reflecting on the message of the song, examining our motives, and remaining willing to grow in our relationship with God. This does not mean that a singer must feel spiritually perfect before participating. We all have areas where we need God’s grace and continued growth. The important thing is to approach the assignment with sincerity rather than carelessness. Our voices may be trained in rehearsal, but our hearts must also be continually directed towards God. “Do not prepare only to sing the song correctly. Prepare your heart to serve the God whose message you are singing.”— Victor Adenola Think about this: If your choir spent three hours perfecting its harmonies but gave no attention to prayer, the Word, or the meaning of the song, what important part of its preparation might be missing? Worship Is More Than the Sound We Produce One of the greatest dangers in church music is confusing musical excellence with spiritual depth. A beautiful sound can create an atmosphere of excitement. A powerful arrangement can capture attention. A skilled singer can move an audience emotionally. But musical impact alone does not automatically mean that worship has taken place in the hearts of the people. We should therefore ask ourselves: Are we communicating the truth of the song? Are we directing attention towards God or towards ourselves? Are we more concerned about impressing the congregation than serving faithfully? Does our conduct reflect the values we proclaim through our songs? There is nothing wrong with desiring an excellent performance. The problem begins when performance becomes the ultimate goal. “Musical excellence is a valuable tool, but it must never become a substitute for the spiritual purpose it is meant to serve.”— Victor Adenola A choir should pursue excellence without allowing applause, recognition, popularity, or personal ambition to become its motivation. The Altar Begins Before You Reach the Platform We often associate the altar with the physical place where people gather to worship. But for a choir member, preparation for ministry begins long before stepping onto the platform. It begins with the decisions we make when nobody is watching. How do we treat our families? How do we speak to fellow members? How do we respond when corrected? Are we honest in our dealings? Do we pursue peace, forgiveness, and accountability? These questions matter because our spiritual lives cannot be reduced to what happens during a church service. This does not mean that only people who have achieved perfection can minister. If that were the requirement, none of us would qualify. Rather, it means that those who serve should remain teachable, accountable, and committed to spiritual growth. When we discover areas of weakness, we should not hide behind our musical gifts. We should seek God’s help, make necessary corrections, and pursue reconciliation where possible. The platform should be an extension of a life that is continually being shaped by God, not a place where we pretend to be someone we are not. “The platform is not where your spiritual life begins. It is where a part of your preparation becomes visible.”— Victor Adenola Think about this: Who are you becoming outside the church service, and how is that person influencing the way you minister inside the church? Prayer Must Be More Than an Opening Routine Many choirs begin rehearsals with prayer. This is good, but prayer should not become a ritual we complete before moving on to the “real work” of music. Prayer helps us acknowledge our dependence on God. It reminds us that our gifts, opportunities, strength, and ability to serve are not reasons for pride. It also helps us bring our motives, relationships, challenges, and responsibilities before God. A spiritually intentional rehearsal might include: Praying for understanding of the song’s message. Asking God for wisdom and discipline in preparation. Praying for unity among choir members. Seeking humility in the way correction is given and received. Praying for the congregation and the people who may be reached through the ministry. Asking for sensitivity to the needs of others. These practices need not make every rehearsal unnecessarily long. They should make the time we spend together more purposeful. Prayer should also be supported by practical action. If we pray for unity, we must be willing to resolve conflict. If we pray for excellence, we must practise. If we pray for people who are hurting, we must be willing to respond compassionately when we encounter them. “Prayer is not a replacement for preparation; it is part of our dependence on God as we prepare and serve.”— Victor Adenola The Holy Spirit Is Not a Substitute for Musical Discipline Spirituality and musical excellence should not be treated as enemies. Sometimes, people speak as though preparation shows a lack of faith, or as though prayer alone will correct poor timing, inaccurate notes, weak harmonies, and inadequate practice. But careful preparation and dependence on God can work together. A choir can pray and still practise diligently. A singer can trust God and still work on breath control. A music director can seek spiritual direction and still plan rehearsals carefully. We should not use spirituality as an excuse for avoidable musical weaknesses. Neither should we use musical competence as an excuse to neglect spiritual growth. The aim is not to choose between the Spirit and skill, but to develop our skills while remaining spiritually grounded. “Faith does not excuse carelessness. When we understand the value of our assignment, we prepare diligently and depend on God humbly.”— Victor Adenola Think about this: Are you expecting prayer to do what disciplined practice requires, or are you allowing your preparation to become disconnected from your dependence on God? A Spiritually Healthy Choir Must Be a United Choir Psalm 133 celebrates the goodness of brethren dwelling together in unity. For a choir, unity is not merely about standing in the right order or singing the same notes. It is about learning to work together with humility, respect, and a shared purpose. A choir may sing in harmony while its members remain divided by jealousy, competition, resentment, or unresolved conflict. Musical harmony does not automatically guarantee relational harmony. This is why spiritual growth should influence how we treat one another. Members should be willing to apologise, forgive, receive correction, and celebrate one another’s progress. Leaders should also model the attitudes they expect from the choir. Authority should not become a tool for humiliation, and spiritual language should never be used to silence legitimate concerns or avoid accountability. Where reconciliation is needed, it should be pursued honestly and safely. Where serious wrongdoing has occurred, appropriate accountability may also be necessary. A united choir is not a choir without differences. It is a choir committed to handling differences in ways that protect its purpose and respect its members. “A choir cannot consistently communicate a message of love while deliberately nurturing hatred, pride, and division among its members.”— Victor Adenola Remember the Person Who May Be Listening From the Back Let us return to the experience that inspired this series. A man who was contemplating suicide heard a choir rehearsing. He followed the sound to the church, sat at the back, and cried. A minister noticed him and attended to him. Consider the sequence: a choir was rehearsing, the sound reached someone beyond the rehearsal room, the person came closer, and another member of the church community responded. The choir members may not have known he was there. They may not have known what he was facing. Yet, their rehearsal became a point of connection. This is a powerful reminder that our ministry can have an impact beyond what we see. However, we must understand the lesson responsibly. We cannot promise that every song will solve someone’s problem, nor should we assume that music alone is enough to address a crisis. People experiencing serious emotional distress may need compassionate human support, professional care, and immediate help when they are in danger. Think about this: If someone walked into your church today feeling hopeless, would your choir and church community be prepared to offer more than a song? Build a Culture of Intentional Rehearsal How can a choir put these principles into practice? Start with small, consistent changes. Before rehearsal: Read the lyrics and understand their spiritual message. Spend personal time in prayer and the Word. Practise your assigned parts before arriving. Come with a willingness to learn and serve. During rehearsal: Begin with a clear purpose and appropriate prayer. Explain the meaning and purpose of the songs. Correct musical errors respectfully. Encourage unity, discipline, and active listening. Make room for brief reflection when it will genuinely help the choir understand its assignment. After rehearsal: Review what needs improvement. Follow up on unresolved musical or relational issues. Reflect on your own attitude and contribution. Pray for the congregation and the wider community the choir serves. During ministration: Focus on communicating the song’s message truthfully. Avoid unnecessary competition and distractions. Remain attentive to the service and the congregation. Serve with humility, discipline, and sensitivity. The objective is not to make every rehearsal complicated. It is to make every rehearsal purposeful. A choir does not become spiritually mature in one meeting. It grows through repeated decisions to seek God, understand the message, practise diligently, and treat people with care. -Victor Adenola A Final Challenge to Choir Leaders and Members To the choir leader: Do not measure the success of your choir only by how well it sounds on Sunday. Ask whether your members are growing in understanding, discipline, unity, and responsibility. To the music director: Do not separate musical instruction from the purpose of the ministry. Teach the notes, explain the message, and model the discipline you expect. To the choir member: Do not leave all spiritual responsibility to your pastor, choir leader, or music director. Your personal relationship with God matters. Your preparation matters. Your conduct matters. To the church: Do not celebrate the choir only when it performs well. Support its growth, provide healthy leadership, and build a community that values both excellence and compassion. And to every person involved in gospel music: remember that the gift is not the final destination. It is a means through which you can serve. “The measure of our ministry is not simply how powerfully we sing in public, but how faithfully we prepare, how sincerely we serve, and how responsibly we treat the people entrusted to our care.”— Victor Adenola Conclusion: Let the Song Continue Beyond the Rehearsal A rehearsal ends. A service closes. The instruments are packed away, the microphones are switched off, and the choir members return to their daily responsibilities. But the purpose of the ministry should not end there. The lessons of prayer, discipline, unity, humility, and compassion must continue to shape the way we live and serve. We may never know the full impact of a song. We may never meet every person who has been encouraged by our music. But we can choose to prepare with understanding, serve with sincerity, and remain open to the needs of others. Let us build choirs that are musically competent and spiritually grounded. Let us pursue excellence without pride, practise discipline without cruelty, and preach hope through our songs while demonstrating compassion through our actions. Above all, let us remember that we are not merely gathering to produce a sound. We are gathering to serve God and communicate a message that deserves to be understood and handled responsibly. The rehearsal room is not just where the song is perfected. It is where the people carrying the song prepare for their responsibility. CALL TO ACTION: WHAT WILL YOU CHANGE AFTER READING THIS? This series must become more than something we read, share, or admire. Its value will be seen in what we choose to do differently. I invite every choir leader, music director, choir member, pastor, and gospel music minister to take these three steps: Examine your preparation. Ask yourself honestly: Am I preparing only my voice, or am I also nurturing my spiritual life, character, and understanding of the message I sing? Change one thing in your next rehearsal. Introduce a meaningful reflection on the song’s message. Improve the way corrections are given. Make room for prayer with purpose. Address a lingering conflict. Or establish a clearer standard for personal preparation. Start a conversation with your choir. Share this series with your choir leader, music director, or fellow members. Discuss what it means to build a choir that serves with spiritual understanding, musical excellence, unity, and compassion. Then agree on one practical change you will implement together. Do not wait until your choir is perfect before you begin. Start with the people you have, the resources available, and the next rehearsal you can influence. Here is my challenge to you: Before your next rehearsal, take five minutes to pray, reflect on the purpose of your ministry, and ask God to help you become more intentional about the way you serve. Then let your actions support that prayer. If this series has challenged your thinking, share it with another choir leader or music minister who needs the conversation. And I would love to hear from you: What is one change you will make in your choir to ensure that your rehearsals prepare not just the song, but also the people who will sing it? Share your thoughts, discuss them with your team, and put one practical step into action. Let us move beyond rehearsing songs. Let us build choirs that understand their message, honour God through their preparation, and serve people with sincerity.
